summary:
Andhra Pradesh stands under India's national framework, and no Andhra Pradesh-specific recognition regime or deviation from that framework is sourced. The operative baseline is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill 2026, which India's Parliament passed in both houses and which awaited presidential assent as of 26 March 2026. The amendment removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals, excludes self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition. Human Rights Watch calls the change a major setback that strips thousands of rights and increases risk; as national law it sets the recognition baseline a visitor faces in this state.

The government presents the amendment as widening access to welfare benefits, while critics and opposition parties, who protested alongside the LGBTQ community, say it excludes transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people. Recognition remains uneven across India amid continuing discrimination in education, healthcare and formal employment.

Entry and stay sit on a mixed baseline. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers sexual orientation and gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units. The replacement of the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 2024 removed gender-identity-specific sexual offences that had protected trans persons, and trans people fear a rise in assaults as a result.

Identity checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student was stopped at Chennai International Airport by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by that force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
India's estimated two million transgender people form the population context for the 2026 amendment's reach. The Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling remains the reference point activists invoke against the new recognition limits, and rights campaigners including Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist.

Welfare infrastructure varies sharply between Indian states: Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha operate transgender welfare boards with housing subsidies, free surgery in public hospitals and pensions, while other states offer only partial benefits. Andhra Pradesh's own welfare provision for trans residents is not sourced in this inventory.
localsOnly:
For residents of Andhra Pradesh, the 2026 amendment's medical-certification requirement governs identity-document applications, and the exclusion of self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people from the recognition scheme affects access to documents and welfare schemes tied to legal recognition.

Resident-facing protections include the Madras High Court's 2021 S. Sushma guidelines on police conduct and conversion therapy (issued for Tamil Nadu), the National Medical Commission's 2022 conversion therapy ban, and the Ayushman Bharat expansion of April 2024 covering transition-related healthcare. The Ministry of Finance's August 2024 clarification on joint bank accounts and beneficiary designation applies nationally.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill 2026 had received presidential assent as of the latest sourced date is unresolved; the inventory records it awaiting assent on 26 March 2026.

Andhra Pradesh-specific enforcement practice, police conduct data, welfare-board existence, and intersex-surgery incidence in this state are not sourced in the inventory and remain unverified here.
